fixes.explanation: The text says the opposite, friend. The Teacher tells himself to enjoy what is good, and then he says, “…it proved to be futile.” So his test with pleasure came out empty.

That's what he says. “I said of laughter, ‘It is folly,’ and of pleasure, ‘What does it accomplish?’” (Ecclesiastes 2:2). Now, I take laughter seriously around here, friend, so I'm just reading you the verse and keeping my mustache folded.
Laughter might do you good, but that's not the Teacher's word here. He says of laughter, “It is folly…” and he asks of pleasure, “What does it accomplish?” Medicine isn't the word he uses.
A gift is a nice thought, but the Teacher doesn't say it. He says of laughter, “It is folly…” and he asks of pleasure, “What does it accomplish?” Folly is the word he uses for laughter here.
That's right. He says he sought to cheer his body with wine and to embrace folly, “…my mind still guiding me with wisdom…” So his head stayed in the driver's seat while he did it.
That's right. He says, “Anything my eyes desired, I did not deny myself. I refused my heart no pleasure.” So he denied himself nothing his eyes desired. Me, I have to hide the cookie tin from myself.
